content:
The reviews are in for first lady Melania Trump’s new Amazon TV series, and they’re not exactly filled with the kinds of quotes seen on posters.

From “utter garbage” to “entirely skippable,” the two-part “Melania, The Series” is the opposite of a critical darling ― and that’s when it’s reviewed at all.

A number of critics and publications seem to have skipped it entirely.

The series is a follow-up to “Melania,” the documentary film released earlier this year by Amazon, which paid $75 million for production, distribution and promotion. At least $10 million of that went to Melania herself, according to President Donald Trump’s financial disclosure.

Based on the reviews, however, it seems like the company didn’t get its money’s worth.

Stuart Heritage of The Guardian gave the series no stars ― but had plenty to say about the “dead-eyed advert,” especially an extended sequence on the placement of a brooch that “goes on for so much longer than you would expect it to.”

Even at 1.5x speed, Heritage writes, it took forever.

“I ended up falling into a catatonic fugue state, watching it,” he wrote. “I might still be watching it now. The show has robbed me of my capacity to discern the boundaries of time and space.”

He adds: “Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry.”

But the review itself is still pretty harsh.

“Think of it less as a fly-on-the-wall documentary, more as an audition reel to be a supervillain in the next Minions film,” Singh wrote.

The Hollywood Reporter hasn’t published a full review, but TV critic Daniel Fienberg, in the weekend email summary, called the show “utter garbage” and “an artless symphony of sycophancy,” but said the first lady is more comfortable in this show than in the documentary.

“She actually makes a joke or two,” he wrote. “Not funny jokes, but whatever.”

She wrote:

“It has no story, no themes, no arc and practically no beginning, middle or end. It just sort of is. It’s an Instagram ad, a PowerPoint presentation, as obsequious and sycophantic to Melania as ChatGPT is to its most loyal users. Even suggesting that it’s reality TV would be too generous. At least reality TV is entertaining.”

The Financial Times dismissed the series as “brazen propaganda” in Imogen West-Knights’ one-star review.

“One of the more troubling possible takeaways from the series is that this is indeed who Melania is: someone not hiding depth, but lacking it,” West-Knights wrote.

MS NOW’s Brian Lowry compared it to the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything,” saying both the Melania film and the TV series could be called “You Can’t See Anything.”

He called the series “an oversize perfume ad.”

Margaret Hartmann of New York said the series contains none of the “basic building blocks of a coherent program” but “only exists because director Brett Ratner had some leftover footage” from the film.

But it’s not without revelations.

Hartmann notes that Trump is asked to name her favorite book.

“My favorite book, it’s of course, ‘Melania,’” the first lady said, referring to her 2024 memoir.
